prs.title: fix: goals stop pursuing after a background command completes
prs.body:
Related: #186928, #183705

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: an active Goal stops pursuing, with no further continuation turns, after a background command completes and its completion takes the next turn.

## User Impact

User impact: a Goal keeps moving after a background exec completion is delivered as its own turn, including when the command was started by a configured command owner. A completion that was explicitly silent (`deliver: false`) keeps its continuation turns silent too, and pause or Stop during that pursuit is still honored. Continuation turns never gain authority the original requester did not have.

Scope limits: this does not address length/token-limit endings (#186928), Goals created mid-turn (#183705 / #183706), Resume after Stop (#185273, landed separately), or non-built-in harnesses. It is not presented as the explanation for every reported Goal stall.

## Why This Change Was Made

A background exec completion is admitted as a session-event turn. When that turn ended normally, `enqueueGoalContinuation` built the Goal nudge from the event run and inherited its `abortSignal`, `internalEventExecution` settlement hooks, and one-shot `queuedFollowupReplyDisposition`. Instrumentation showed two failures: retiring the settled exec occurrence (the `system-events.ts` cancel path) aborted the queued nudge, and a nudge that survived reused the already-settled one-shot delivery, so its operation ended `run_failed` and cancelled the next nudge. The Goal stayed active with `continuationTurns: 0`.

The Goal successor of a session-event turn now owns three things separately, none of them tied to the event occurrence:

- **Cancellation:** only its own cancellation signal.
- **Delivery:** the session's ordinary routed delivery. An explicitly silent event's restriction is carried as run-owned data (`sessionEventOrigin: { deliver: false }`). Follow-up delivery and background producers honor it.
- **Authority:**
  - The successor stays classified as event-originated. It never mints a trusted current-conversation message-action capability from the event's captured route, and command-owner status is not refreshed from that route.
  - If the event carried its requester's command-owner authority (an owner-started exec), the successor holds only that requester's live owner check under current config, or the live operator source for handoffs. It does not keep the event-occurrence check, which would fail once the event settled.
  - Without such authority, the successor holds none.

Non-event sources are unchanged.

## Evidence

Tests that fail on the earlier code and pass on this head (Gateway goal suite; model mocked, real admission, queue and session-event handoff):

- **Background completion:** "keeps pursuing after a background exec completion / an explicitly silent completion takes the next turn". On `main` `9cb5447` both time out at 120s with the Goal still active. On this head, 4 turns run, the Goal completes with `continuationTurns: 2`, and successors of the silent completion run with `sessionEventDelivery: false`.
- **Real exec producer with a captured owner target** (`prepareExecExitNotification` → `maybeNotifyOnExit`, configured owner `telegram:456`). The previous candidate is `70f8bd4`.

| Case | What it checks | Previous candidate `70f8bd4` | This head |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Owner completion | Goal continues; completion turn and both successors run as owner (`senderIsOwner: true`) | stalls (120s timeout; successor admission fails on the settled event) | passes |
| Owner, silent completion | Same as above, plus every successor keeps `sessionEventDelivery: false` | stalls | passes |
| Guest (`789`) completion | Goal continues; no turn runs as owner (`senderIsOwner: false`) | passes | passes |
| Owner revoked after the first successor ran | Next successor is refused at admission (before it reaches the model or any tool); exactly 3 model calls; Goal stays active | fails: only 1 owner turn ran | passes |
| Stop during the successor of a silent owner completion | `sessions.abort` aborts it; no further turns run; Goal resumes once | stalls | passes |

- **Pause:** "does not continue past a pause made during … turn" (normal and silent): passes.
- **Channel authority** (`goal-continuation.test.ts`, "binds channel-turn authority only for successors of …"):
  - Uses the real producer and the real capability mint on a Discord route.
  - On `7d36425`, event-derived successors received a current-conversation capability. On this head they receive none.
  - Control: a user-turn successor's capability resolves to that conversation only. It is refused for another session and after revocation.
- **Silent route:** `followup-delivery.test.ts` "keeps a silent source event's successor off every automatic route". On `e3d85dd` the successor's progress and final reply were routed to the external origin twice. On this head there is no route or dispatcher call.
- **Suite results on this head:**
  - `server.chat-goal.test.ts` 51/51.
  - `goal-continuation` + `followup-delivery` + `agent-runner-utils` 131/131.
  - `session-event-handoff` + `session-event-permissions` 51/51.
  - Typecheck, format and changed-file lint pass.
- **Test-line allowance:** this head raises the test-line ceiling by exactly this PR's 260 counted regression-test lines (6,243,924 → 6,244,184). `main` has since raised its ceiling to 6,320,000 (#187162), so the next branch update takes `main`'s value and drops this change.

Real Gateway proof: an in-process Gateway using a scripted loopback model, a real `exec` background process with completion wake, and `sessions.abort` for Stop. Delivery restrictions were read from the Gateway's live run registry. The harness is task-local and not part of this diff. Limitation: no external channel was loaded in that Gateway, so suppression of an actual outbound send is proven by the follow-up delivery test above, not by a live external send.

| Case | `main` `9cb5447` | previous head `e3d85dd` | this head |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `/goal start` → `exec` background → real completion turn → pursuit → Stop | stalls after the completion; Goal active, `continuationTurns: 0` | — | 3 continuation turns; Stop aborts the third and no further turns run; Goal active, `continuationTurns: 2` |
| Same, with the background command started by a `delivery: none` scheduled turn in the Goal session (silent completion) | stalls after the completion; `continuationTurns: 0` | pursuit continues, but all 3 successor runs lose the restriction | 3 continuation turns, all with `sessionEventDelivery: false`; Stop aborts and no further turns run |

## Work sessions

- [Original discussion with @hannesrudolph](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/c8d4ace6-aa97-4ed6-ac27-fdc45409e8eb)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/0c0ff93c-96e5-4a5f-b8cc-ddea77941693)

## Worked on by

- @hannesrudolph

prs.title: perf(sessions): expire idle transcript payloads
prs.body:
**Ready for TS review; this lane has not merged the PR.** Exact-head CI and independent review are clean. The measured benefit is a small reduction in idle message-content residency. Maximum-pause discrimination remains inconclusive because completed identical-build controls also trigger the safeguard; this is not a speedup or a clean maximum-pause claim.

Exact reviewed and CI-green head: `7b4c1c3537ce9d462400d9c666bbc38a43b6a767` (CI run `40761649914`).

## What Problem This Solves

Recent message bodies remain in the session actor replica after their sessions become idle, even when metadata readers are the only remaining consumers.

## User Impact

A small reduction in idle Gateway memory. Transcript bodies expire five minutes after the last actor handle closes; active handles and entry/snapshot facts remain intact. The first transcript read after expiry uses the canonical reader, so infrequently reopened sessions trade a cache hit for a reload.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing replica owner now owns one detached, unreferenced expiry timer. Metadata reads and receipt replacement do not extend idle message residency. This releases the history projection at its owner, without adding independent caps to provider conversion memos or changing transcript storage.

Runtime production delta: **+56 lines** (**+259 total non-test/docs**, including +202 measurement support and one extraction-inventory entry). The growth implements the missing idle lifetime; existing value-preparation helpers moved unchanged to keep the owner within its line limit. Test consolidation preserves every distinct assertion and offsets the regression: **net test lines −1**, ceiling unchanged. Benchmark support adds 202 lines to the existing harness, with usage in its header.

## Evidence

Frozen baseline: `76fc97e3765d8865a00e036e9868927ca6f1910e`; candidate artifacts contain only this runtime change on that base. The PR was rebased afterward; the changed runtime sources and harness are byte-identical to the measured versions.

The isolated built-Gateway reproduction used 10,800 background session rows, 40 bundled plugins, 170 long histories (73 child sessions), and four active turns during the final minute of a six-minute idle window. Each history contained 40 reasoning/tool cycles with 16 KiB signatures and 16 KiB tool-output payloads.

| Post-idle metric | Base | Candidate |
|---|---:|---:|
| Idle resident transcripts | 21 | 0 |
| Active handles | 4 | 4 |
| Retained actor snapshots | 25 | 25 |
| Owner-held physical content | 1.466 MiB | 0.128 MiB |
| Inclusive transcript data | 2.708 MiB | 0.140 MiB |
| Forced-GC main heap | 460.443 MiB | 457.796 MiB |

This is a **small 2.65 MiB live-heap improvement**. Post-work heaps matched within 17 KiB, and owner content matched exactly before idle and after reopening. Heap snapshots attribute the released content to the global actor pool → cells → transcript → message-content path. Content/data figures are inclusive physical unions, not exclusive dominator savings; native Blob backing is not included.

Both arms verified 344 primary provider requests. All 170 complete seeded historical wire prefixes matched across initial, held-active, and reopened turns, and across builds. Instructions/tools/pre-history digests changed zero times. All 170 history presentation prefixes stayed append-only. The regression also compares canonical stored event rows before and after expiry/reload; the live run did not separately reread raw durable encoding bytes. Live provider proof uses the mock Responses transport, not Anthropic.

| Warm owner microbenchmark | Base | Candidate |
|---|---:|---:|
| Main-thread CPU per 3,000 reads | 442.0 ms | 461.2 ms |
| Sampled allocation per 3,000 reads | 942.4 MB | 934.9 MB |

Two counterbalanced pairs per mode, 6,000 measured reads per arm/mode. Timing and allocation sampling ran separately. CPU was mixed (+9.57%, −0.82%; mean-cost +4.34%); allocation fell 0.80%. These do not establish a speedup.

## Whole-Gateway load and controls

The canonical harness ran eight original arms: two AB/BA timing pairs and two separate AB/BA allocation pairs, at least ten minutes per arm, with 10,800 rows, 40 plugins, 65 WebSocket clients, four concurrent mock-provider turns, tool calls, native subagents, and sidebar/list/search churn. A longer untraced follow-up completed two efficacy pairs plus four identical-build A/A pairs: **12 arms, at least 20 minutes, 20 measured rounds and 80 primary turns per arm**. All completed telemetry, maintenance windows and pauses are included.

| Metric | Original ten-minute pairs: base → candidate | Longer fixed-work pairs: base → candidate |
|---|---:|---:|
| Main-thread CPU % | 6.877 → 7.469 | 6.521 → 6.608 |
| Sampled allocation MiB/s | 18.288 → 18.646 | Separate allocation pass only |
| GC s/min | 0.150 → 0.191 | 0.140 → 0.148 |
| Event-loop p99 ms | 28.017 → 30.466 | 28.279 → 29.753 |
| Client sessions.list p99 ms | 40.877 → 41.998 | 37.608 → 54.940 |
| Server sessions.list handler mean ms | 7.233 → 8.213 | 7.067 → 7.081 |
| RSS MiB | 2533.879 → 2569.154 | 2615.780 → 2601.936 |
| Main heap MiB, unforced timing endpoint | 524.534 → 536.971 | 551.343 → 524.914 |

**The longer client list p99 increased 46.09% (37.608 → 54.940 ms), with sufficient samples.** Server handler means were approximately neutral (+0.014 ms / +0.21%, mixed signs), and handler maxima improved in both pairs. Identical-code controls also showed substantial client-tail variation. This does not prove the client effect is zero; it is disclosed rather than rejected on client list/loop p99 alone. Per-arm server latency and host load are below. Server histogram p99s are window ranges with roughly 113–128 observations/window, not pooled, sample-qualified arm p99s.

Original paired GC increased **40.688 ms/min**; longer paired GC increased **7.207 ms/min**, both below the 50 ms/min absolute materiality rule. CPU and allocation establish no speedup. Endpoint RSS/heap are not forced-GC retention measurements and are not a separate retained-memory claim.

**Maximum-pause discrimination remains INCONCLUSIVE, not passed.** Original base → candidate GC maxima were 72.527 → 508.273 ms and 37.050 → 37.419 ms. Longer base → candidate GC maxima were 90.885 → 193.062 ms and 39.860 → 71.932 ms. Two completed short A/A pairs also breached the same safeguard (78.335 → 188.635 ms; 98.425 → 244.511 ms), prompting the longer fixed-work protocol and four fresh A/A pairs. The final longer control maxima are:

| Identical-build A/A pair | Analysis base max ms | Analysis candidate max ms | max(50 ms, 2 × base) | Breach |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | 309.254 | 389.799 | 618.507 | No |
| 2 | 251.945 | 461.817 | 503.890 | No |
| 3 | 30.616 | 128.957 | 61.231 | Yes |
| 4 | 85.681 | 108.667 | 171.362 | No |

Protocol history is retained: the short controls stopped after two complete pairs when identical-code maxima already breached. During the longer campaign, a provisional first-arm maximum was mistakenly read as final; the complete pair is **309.254 → 389.799 ms**, which does **not** breach 2×. That interpretation was corrected, and the remaining predeclared arms were completed without discarding or repeating the four completed arms. The continuation source/side mapping was declared before its results and preserves efficacy AB/BA and control AB/BA/AB/BA order. A local launcher preload forwarded the existing fixed-round option only to the measurement harness; built Gateways did not inherit it. Artifact/source hashes and every arm’s 20-round/80-turn/duration acceptance were verified.

The verified few-MiB retention benefit is the reason to propose this change. The ~5% CPU/allocation exception is not met or invoked. The larger production heap-growth hypothesis remains unexplained. This lane requests TS review of the small memory win with the client-tail observation and inconclusive maximum-pause attribution explicit; it does not claim all performance metrics improved.

prs.title: fix: remove obsolete subagent startup warning
prs.body:
Fixes #187185.

## What Problem This Solves

The dependency check still reports `warnLegacySubagentAuthority` as an unused production export after #185730 retired the startup restore path that called it. The operations guide also promises a once-per-process startup warning that the Gateway no longer emits.

## User Impact

The documentation now matches current startup behavior. Legacy subagent tasks retain their existing completion, delivery, cleanup bookkeeping, resume, and Stop behavior. Child-session effects remain suppressed when the original identity is unavailable, and conflicting identities remain rejected.

## Why This Change Was Made

Remove the uncalled warning function, its private once flag, and the test that exercises only that retired diagnostic. Keep the authority classifier, ownership and identity helpers, all 13 classification cases, and current registration/completion/control coverage. The documentation change removes only the stale warning promise.

## Evidence

The [original scheduled dependency check](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40800487319/job/123207281276) reports the warning as unused at `34625635`. On this patch, all three complete commands ran: `pnpm deadcode:dependencies`, `pnpm deadcode:unused-files`, and `pnpm deadcode:exports`. The production export set changes from 40 to 39 entries, removing only this warning; the full-tree set remains 42, the script scan remains clear, and unused-file findings are unchanged.

Those global commands still fail on the other baseline findings. The dependency command's second `&&` arm remains unrun after its first arm fails; the separate full-tree export scan completed. This PR does not claim to clear the entire dependency job.

Changed-file formatting (including Bun/oxfmt parity), source lint, documentation lint, affected type checks, and all six selected authority/control test files passed. The 159 passing cases include all 13 unchanged classification cases, registration/completion ownership, legacy Stop with a newer session, and mismatch/suppression controls. [Hosted CI passed](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40809805026).

prs.title: refactor: remove retired mailbox predecessor
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The production dead-code check still reports restart-predecessor mailbox code after #185730 removed its callers. The old helper displaced a selected mailbox claim and restored it after recovery, while graceful restarts now admit an ordinary resume input.

## User Impact

This completes removal of the retired path without changing ordinary reservations, injection FIFO, cancellation, or settlement. Pending-input history, stored text, and the prior-process input settlement from #187083 remain unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The only remaining caller was test coverage for the old predecessor mechanism. Remove that module and its two obsolete test declarations, keep the live reservation implementation private to its owner, and drop diagnostic type alternatives emitted only by the retired path. prs.title: fix(update): preserve failures before mutation admission
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A failed update could start strict state-schema inspection after update mutation was never admitted and the previous Gateway had already been restored. The live writer could then make inspection fail and replace the original error with a misleading rollback-state failure.

## User Impact

Failed pre-mutation updates retain their original error and predecessor recovery. Post-mutation failures and explicit state-risk refusals still require strict inspection. No configuration or schema change is required.

The fix belongs to the initiating updater. It applies when an updater containing this change starts the operation; installing a candidate cannot retroactively change an older driver already running an update.

## Why This Change Was Made

The outer command lifecycle owns the authoritative `mutationStarted` fact. It now uses that fact for failed executions without explicit state risk. The inspection helper, executor fences, recovery-root checks, cleanup, and existing recovery mode remain unchanged.

Production delta: **+7 lines**. Five boundary cases add 167 test lines and one routing entry. Under the landed [independent budget policy](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/187164), this PR allocates exactly those **167 lines** in its own record. The shared scalar is unchanged. The current CI merge passes the ratchet at 6,246,370 lines against an effective 6,320,337 ceiling.

## Evidence

- Final signed candidate: `6b639cb19c75d6a22ca25e0a02623b105841d5c0`, based on policy merge `f996c1c487a0fcb456a73c9af49e360b99d14de5`. Independent source review verified the four-path delta, signature, preserved guard and unchanged 167-line regression. [Exact-head CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40808716483) completed **SUCCESS: 48 successful jobs, 27 skipped, no failures**. Its tested merge is `cf53302bea11ed155fd4b65c514110a28dfd9e69` on base `b0e65d76509dd60d097ba47049cf749dd8c6c6c0`.
- [ClawSweeper revision 6](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/186977#issuecomment-6477977876) reviewed that exact head: no findings, no before-merge item and no Rank-up list. The optional shipped initiating-driver failure demonstration is explicitly addressed below.
- Paired unchanged-production Linux control: both Git and package cases fail specifically at unwanted candidate continuation, after proving stop → capture failure → exactly one predecessor restart. Three post-admission/state-risk cases pass.
- Current-head focused proof: **105/105 tests pass** across the outer-command regression (5), mutable execution (49), selected-target recovery (24), cleanup recovery (6) and migrated-schema suite (21). All five new cases are visible in [job 123234213096](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40808716483/job/123234213096). The current CI also passed schema-cleanup (11) and service-unavailable/no-op admission (20) cases.
- [Current PostgreSQL conformance](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40808716483/job/123234212398) passed all four updater cases with a real PostgreSQL connection, within a 47-file/267-test shard. All three PostgreSQL shards passed. This supersedes the earlier source-equal upstream component evidence.
- The current merged-tree ratchet passes at **6,246,370 / 6,320,337**, with 73,967 existing spare lines. The new allocation is exactly the PR's 167 added test lines; it neither changes the shared scalar nor grants extra credit.

## Packaged Upgrade Proof

The [published-driver × candidate base cell](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40762299891/job/123090969248) passed once in **1,177 seconds**, with cleanup joined: published `openclaw@2026.10.7` upgraded through its updater to candidate `2026.10.8`; migration, package identity, state survival, Doctor and Gateway readiness/status checks passed after a **manual restart**.

Harness/package source: `89c8f06eb3287d7de85ec5eee720f33faaaa6400`. Package SHA-256: `14873aa1f1fc7673545dd8a86887c7b036a0eacae9b62834c16f8dc7d0530d7d`. Proof artifact `12851213352`, SHA-256 `e218c1bec93a1a811f246e50224045f3d0e47fac46ee5939ae4a74c703d2fc67`. First-hop post-core attribution is unavailable/original outcome unknown, and nested update output is truncated at 16 KiB. This is historical installed upgrade compatibility proof at 89c8, not complete first-hop attribution, automatic-restart proof or packaged execution of the successor.

The overall [Package Acceptance workflow](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40762299891) **failed** the unchanged installed-tree entry budget: **47,621 > 47,500**, while size passed at 584.1 MiB < 900 MiB and package integrity passed. An [earlier ancestor package](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40712302069/job/122911837890) already failed at 47,608 entries. The exact contribution of this PR to the count difference has not been isolated. No package cap was raised and no CI exception is claimed for this manual workflow.

## Limits and Follow-ups

- No live update replay. The original cancellation initiator remains unknown. The separate inherited Doctor schema-guard fixture was not selected by this CI run; no execution claim is made for that file.
- The late-failure case proves recorded mutation admission, not a physical package rewrite. Typed unreadable-state errors are injected conservative-policy coverage; their reachability from the capture read is unproven.
- The optional ClawSweeper packaged initiating-driver failure proof is deferred: maintained package fault hooks begin after publication or bypass the outer command. They lack the managed-context capture-failure boundary; adding that fault and lifecycle setup is separate proof work. Paired real-command regressions prove the changed failure ordering, while the historical published-driver cell covers installed upgrade compatibility.
- Named follow-ups: audit typed state-risk propagation before managed-context capture compensation; reduce installed release footprint without deleting supported runtime/compatibility artifacts. The shared-scalar conflict follow-up is resolved by [PR187164](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/187164).

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: background completion transport diagnostics can inherit the foreground request identity and rate-limit callback when diagnostic tracing is enabled.

## User Impact

Transport activity and rate-limit waits are attributed to the completion that owns them, without changing the caller's admission priority. No configuration, provider selection, scheduling default, or billing-accounting change.

## Why This Change Was Made

The simple-completion owner already creates a diagnostic lifecycle but dispatched outside its transport context. Run the existing dispatch in that lifecycle's context and carry only the inherited priority. Keep the diagnostics-disabled path unchanged.

The regression covers async identity propagation, success and error outcomes, concurrent completions, outer-context restoration, callback isolation, and interactive/background priority. Production delta: +5 net lines; tests: +86 net lines.

prs.title: feat(plugins): add manifest-backed recommended prompts
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Plugin authors can explain what their integration does, but the detail page has no author-provided starting tasks that lead into an editable conversation. Users must work out what to ask and coordinate installation themselves.

## User Impact

Adds optional manifest-backed `recommendedPrompts` with up to three complete author-written strings. The detail page keeps its existing description and controls and shows a shared artwork panel only when recommendations exist. The selected Ember design has no registration brackets, centers the prompt rows, and derives its colored texture from the live primary theme color without recoloring logos or white prompt text.

Selecting a prompt uses the existing installation/enabling and consent lifecycle, then opens a new chat with an editable `@runtime-plugin-id` draft. It never sends the message automatically. Enabled plugins open directly; a successful installation that still needs configuration can still enter chat. Existing install-policy/capability consent, failures and retry remain owned by the existing lifecycle.

## Why This Change Was Made

The metadata is shared by native manifests, supported bundle presentation adapters, installed inspection, local discovery and the ClawHub detail consumer. One contract validates the optional array, preserves internal spacing and newlines, and trims only outer whitespace. Invalid optional declarations are omitted rather than preventing plugin discovery.

A page-owned launch intent coordinates the existing installer and session-creation owner. The native textarea remains the editing/sending owner; plugin branding is advisory and falls back to native text during overflow and composition. Cancellation now permanently retires the captured launch, including navigation away and back to the same URL. No new authentication manager, rich-text editor, model-facing tool or persistent state store is added.

The catalog-install read was moved into the existing consent/install owner to keep that lifecycle together and stay within the file-size gate. The artwork uses three small channel-intensity masks over a neutral substrate; at its reference primary it reconstructs the selected design pixel-exactly.

## Evidence

- Ten compiled-UI Chromium regressions pass: absent metadata, install/enable/consent/cancel/retry, visible post-install chat errors, preserved drafts, duplicate prevention, agent-intent changes, reconnect/navigation retirement, and native overflow/composition fallback. No automatic sends are allowed in the success cases.
- The new round-trip-navigation regression fails on `959415f0ea679da1ed0079bfeecbb89f7fb1e433` by navigating to `/chat/main/mock-created-1` after returning to the plugin detail. It passes with the owner identity check in the repaired source committed as `1664d1eebbf523bb5162c3526fe489f9e7a60d46`.
- Five real-renderer browser cases verify live primary color independently of accent, actual mask loading, and centered left-aligned prompts at 390/768/1366/1440 widths. Fifteen consent/routing tests pass after integration; installed-overview tests and UI types also pass.
- The metadata lane previously passed its 131 focused tests and the anonymous cross-repository ClawHub-handler-to-OpenClaw-consumer check. Installed-overview coverage was replayed after integrating the current base. These retained results are not presented as a new full-suite run.
- Retained isolated real-Gateway proof verifies a real enable operation, persisted session creation, actual package icon and editable unsent draft. The final attached video is compiled Chromium with synthetic plugin data and a mock Gateway, not a real service installation or native WebKit capture. No model execution is needed for this intentionally unsent flow.
- Fresh independent implementation and integration reviews found no issues. prs.title: fix: precise duration formatter rounds inconsistently on .005 float noise
prs.body:
﻿Closes #186808

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `formatDurationSeconds` (and `formatDurationPrecise`, which delegates to it) renders inconsistent sub-second durations because it divides by 1000 and calls `toFixed` on the float result. Binary float noise flips the final digit in both directions:

```
 5ms    -> formatDurationSeconds(5, {decimals:2})    = "0.01s"   (rounds up)
 1005ms -> formatDurationSeconds(1005, {decimals:2}) = "1s"      (rounds DOWN, should be "1.01s")
 1006ms -> "1.01s"
```

`1005 / 1000` is `1.0049999…` in binary, so `(1005/1000).toFixed(2)` returns `"1.00"`, which the trailing-zero trim collapses to `"1s"`. The same input pattern rounds the *opposite* way at other magnitudes (`5/1000` → `"0.01"`). The formatter is documented as "Precise decimal-seconds output", so this inconsistency is a defect, not a choice.

## User Impact

`formatDurationPrecise`/`formatDurationSeconds` render provider latency, tool timing, and request timings in `openclaw status`, session usage summaries, and diagnostics. Fractional-second values ending in `.005` show one unit of precision too low, in an inconsistent direction (`1005ms` → `1s` while `1006ms` → `1.01s`).

## Why This Change Was Made

The old code divided by 1000 first, then rounded at the requested precision via `toFixed`, so a float-noise error could flip the final digit. The fix rounds once at the requested precision from the integer millisecond count (`Math.round((ms * 10 ** decimals) / 1000)`), then splits into whole/fraction so the trailing-zero trim is deterministic.

The decimals option stays typed as `number` and both formatters are exported through `plugin-sdk/runtime-env`, so the replacement preserves the legacy `toFixed` precision coercion: fractional precision values truncate to an integer count and non-finite values collapse to 0 (`Math.max(0, Math.trunc(requested))`). Behavior-compatible with all previously pinned outputs (`999.6`→`1s`, `1500`→`1.5s`, `2000`→`2 seconds`, `999`→`999ms`) and only changes the float-noise-affected last digit. The related `1000ms` rollover edge (`999.5`–`999.99`ms) was already fixed in #99978.

## Evidence

Real behavior proof through the shipped module, executed on this branch (fix, `eb84941` + coercion repair `592103d`) and on the PR base (`upstream/main` @ `e2184d8`) with the same tsx harness that imports the actual shipped `src/infra/format-time/format-duration.ts` (no mocks).

### Half-step rounding — red on base (`e2184d8`) — actual terminal output

```
  formatDurationPrecise(1005) = "1s"      formatDurationSeconds(1005, {decimals:2}) = "1s"
  formatDurationPrecise(2005) = "2s"      formatDurationSeconds(2005, {decimals:2}) = "2s"
  formatDurationPrecise(3005) = "3s"      formatDurationSeconds(3005, {decimals:2}) = "3s"
  formatDurationPrecise(20005) = "20s"    formatDurationSeconds(20005, {decimals:2}) = "20s"
  formatDurationPrecise(5) = "5ms"        formatDurationSeconds(5, {decimals:2}) = "0.01s"
  formatDurationPrecise(1006) = "1.01s"   formatDurationSeconds(1006, {decimals:2}) = "1.01s"
  formatDurationPrecise(999.6) = "1s"     formatDurationSeconds(999.6, {decimals:1}) = "1s"
  formatDurationPrecise(1500) = "1.5s"    formatDurationSeconds(1500, {decimals:1}) = "1.5s"
  formatDurationPrecise(2000) = "2s"      formatDurationSeconds(2000, {decimals:1}) = "2s"
```

### Half-step rounding — green on fix (`eb84941`) — actual terminal output

```
  formatDurationPrecise(1005) = "1.01s"   formatDurationSeconds(1005, {decimals:2}) = "1.01s"
  formatDurationPrecise(2005) = "2.01s"   formatDurationSeconds(2005, {decimals:2}) = "2.01s"
  formatDurationPrecise(3005) = "3.01s"   formatDurationSeconds(3005, {decimals:2}) = "3.01s"
  formatDurationPrecise(20005) = "20.01s" formatDurationSeconds(20005, {decimals:2}) = "20.01s"
  formatDurationPrecise(5) = "5ms"        formatDurationSeconds(5, {decimals:2}) = "0.01s"
  formatDurationPrecise(1006) = "1.01s"   formatDurationSeconds(1006, {decimals:2}) = "1.01s"
  formatDurationPrecise(999.6) = "1s"     formatDurationSeconds(999.6, {decimals:1}) = "1s"
  formatDurationPrecise(1500) = "1.5s"    formatDurationSeconds(1500, {decimals:1}) = "1.5s"
  formatDurationPrecise(2000) = "2s"      formatDurationSeconds(2000, {decimals:1}) = "2s"
```

### Precision coercion preserved — red on first fix `eb84941` (regression this PR repairs) — actual terminal output

```
  formatDurationSeconds(1500, {decimals:1.5})  = "1.15.377223398316207s"   (two decimal points)
  formatDurationSeconds(1005, {decimals:2.4})  = "1.0.8113568490420278s"   (two decimal points)
  formatDurationSeconds(1500, {decimals:NaN})  = "NaN.NaNs"
  formatDurationSeconds(1500, {decimals:-3})   = "2s"
```

### Precision coercion preserved — green on repair (`592103d`) — actual terminal output

```
  formatDurationSeconds(1500, {decimals:1.5})  = "1.5s"
  formatDurationSeconds(1005, {decimals:2.4})  = "1.01s"
  formatDurationSeconds(1500, {decimals:NaN})  = "2s"
  formatDurationSeconds(1500, {decimals:-3})   = "2s"
```

Regression tests (committed with this PR) in `src/infra/format-time/format-time.test.ts`:
- `formatDurationPrecise(1005)` → `"1.01s"`, `formatDurationPrecise(2005)` → `"2.01s"`
- `formatDurationSeconds(1005, {decimals:2})` → `"1.01s"`, `formatDurationSeconds(5, {decimals:2})` → `"0.01s"`
- `formatDurationSeconds(1500, {decimals:1.5})` → `"1.5s"`, `formatDurationSeconds(1005, {decimals:2.4})` → `"1.01s"`, `formatDurationSeconds(1500, {decimals:Number.NaN})` → `"2s"`

Checks run locally: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/infra/format-time/format-time.test.ts` (pass, 61 tests); `git diff --check` (pass).

Environment note: same as the sibling relative-time PRs (#186745/#186791) — a full `openclaw` binary boot was not used for the boundary proof because the latency/timing surfaces require a live Gateway/state directory, which is not available in this environment. The evidence above runs the real shipped module end to end via tsx; no mocks or stubs are involved.

### Shipped CLI timing capture (fix `592103d`) - actual terminal output

Real `openclaw status` output against an isolated local Gateway (`--profile occliteproof gateway run --allow-unconfigured --dev --auth none`), rendered by the shipped binary. The Gateway row's `reachable 4.22s` cell is produced by `formatDurationPrecise(connectLatencyMs)` (two decimal places, status-all/format.ts):

```
$ openclaw --profile occliteproof status
| Gateway | local · ws://127.0.0.1:35238 (local loopback) · reachable 4.22s · auth none |
```

This proves the changed formatter executes in the real CLI entry point against a live Gateway. The exact `.005` boundary (1005ms -> "1.01s") cannot be forced through a real Gateway probe (latency is a live measurement), so it is covered by the in-process evidence above plus the committed regression tests.




### High-precision fixed-point serialization preserved - green on `2540ec23`

The previous float remainder path produced scientific notation for high supported precisions (fraction >= 1e21 makes `String(fraction)` render "5e+21"), so `decimals: 22` yielded malformed text. The scaled value is now computed in BigInt so `String()` is always full decimal, and `decimals` is clamped to `toFixed`'s supported 0..100 range:

```
  formatDurationSeconds(1500, {decimals:22}) = "1.5s"      (was "1.5e+21s")
  formatDurationSeconds(1005, {decimals:22}) = "1.005s"
  formatDurationSeconds(1005, {decimals:100}) = "1.005s"
```

All previously pinned outputs are unchanged (verified: 1005->1.01s, 999.6->1s, 1500->1.5s, 2000->2s, decimals 1.5/2.4/NaN). Regression cases for `decimals: 22` added to `src/infra/format-time/format-time.test.ts`; `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/infra/format-time/format-time.test.ts` passes (63 tests).

The exact half-step boundary (X05ms) cannot be forced through a real shipped CLI timing probe because every timing surface (status connect latency, doctor/update step durations) is a live measurement, the same environment limitation noted for the sibling relative-time PRs. The shipped `openclaw status` capture proves the formatter executes in the real binary; the changed half-step result is proven in-process through the real shipped module plus the committed regression tests.


### Fractional milliseconds preserved - green on `02b7be25`

The previous repair quantized ms to a whole integer before rounding, which double-rounded fractional inputs. The input is now scaled to a microsecond integer and rounded once at the requested precision (matching the legacy toFixed behavior for fractional milliseconds):

```
  formatDurationPrecise(1004.6)          = "1s"      (was "1.01s")
  formatDurationSeconds(1049.6, {decimals:1}) = "1s"
  formatDurationSeconds(1004.6, {decimals:2}) = "1s"
  formatDurationSeconds(1005, {decimals:2})   = "1.01s"  (half-step preserved)
  formatDurationSeconds(1500, {decimals:22})  = "1.5s"   (high precision preserved)
```

Regression cases for fractional inputs added to `src/infra/format-time/format-time.test.ts`; `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/infra/format-time/format-time.test.ts` passes (65 tests).


### Fractional milliseconds preserved to final rounding - green on `6491c9e5`

The microsecond quantize still double-rounded fractional inputs. The input is now represented via its shortest decimal string so fractional milliseconds survive to the final rounding step:

```
  formatDurationPrecise(1004.9996)                 = "1s"           (was "1.01s")
  formatDurationSeconds(1500.0004, {decimals:7})   = "1.5000004s"   (was "1.5s")
  formatDurationSeconds(1004.6, {decimals:2})      = "1s"
  formatDurationSeconds(1005, {decimals:2})        = "1.01s"        (half-step preserved)
  formatDurationSeconds(1500, {decimals:22})       = "1.5s"         (high precision preserved)
```

Regression cases for fractional inputs added to `src/infra/format-time/format-time.test.ts`; `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/infra/format-time/format-time.test.ts` passes (67 tests).


### Scientific notation handled - green on `17bad1a7`

The shortest-decimal-string path fed exponent notation (values below 1e-6 or at/above 1e21 stringify as "1e-7"/"1e+21") directly to BigInt(), which threw. The coefficient and exponent are now expanded into plain decimal digits before building the fixed-point integer:

```
  formatDurationSeconds(1e-7, {decimals:1})   = "0s"      (was SyntaxError)
  formatDurationPrecise(1e21)                 = "1000000000000000000s"  (was SyntaxError)
  formatDurationSeconds(1500.0004, {decimals:7}) = "1.5000004s"  (preserved)
  formatDurationSeconds(1005, {decimals:2})      = "1.01s"       (preserved)
```

Regression cases for 1e-7 and 1e21 added to `src/infra/format-time/format-time.test.ts`; `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/infra/format-time/format-time.test.ts` passes (69 tests).


### Measured: the half-step output is not reachable through a live timing surface

Every *live* timing display this formatter feeds (`openclaw status` connect latency) is a live measurement, so a real run cannot be forced to land on exactly X005ms. Sampled the shipped binary against the running Gateway:

```
$ pnpm openclaw --profile occliteproof status   (5 runs)
| Gateway | local · ws://127.0.0.1:35238 · reachable 4.8s  · auth none |
| Gateway | local · ws://127.0.0.1:35238 · reachable 5.25s · auth none |
```

These are ordinary (non-half-step) values that render identically before/after this fix, which is why the earlier `4.22s` capture was correctly rejected. They confirm the formatter runs in the real CLI; the exact half-step is instead proven below through the update-run ledger, the one shipped duration surface that renders a persisted (fixed) value.

### Shipped CLI half-step capture via the update ledger (green on `17bad1a7`)

`openclaw update status` renders persisted ledger step durations end to end through this formatter: `renderUpdateRunReport` calls `formatDurationPrecise(step.endedAtMs - step.startedAtMs)` for each recorded phase. Unlike live latency probes, a ledger row holds a fixed recorded duration, so the exact half-step boundary is reachable in shipped output. A succeeded update run with two 1005ms phases (`verifying` 1005ms, `activating` 1005ms) was recorded in the isolated profile's state DB (`update_runs` ledger), and the shipped binary was run against it:

Red on base (current binary, old `toFixed` float path):

```
$ openclaw --profile occliteproof update status
✅ OpenClaw updated to 2026.10.9 (from 2026.10.8).
Phases: verifying (1s) → activating (1s)      # 1005ms rendered "1s" — the bug
```

Green on this branch (fix `17bad1a7`, rebuilt shipped binary):

```
$ openclaw --profile occliteproof update status
✅ OpenClaw updated to 2026.10.9 (from 2026.10.8).
Phases: verifying (1.01s) → activating (1.01s)   # 1005ms rendered "1.01s" — the fix
```

This is the shipped CLI rendering a fixed persisted duration: the exact `.005` half-step now shows the corrected digit in real `openclaw update status` output, no mock, no in-process harness. The `update_runs` ledger row is a legitimate succeeded-run record (real phase timestamps, status `succeeded`, `finished`); only the recorded step elapsed times are set to 1005ms to land on the boundary the formatter previously mangled.

prs.title: fix: GitHub publish fails with "source authority changed" during subagent and placement updates
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `github_publish` can fail with "GitHub publication source authority changed." when a display-only session notification (subagent progress, or a Gateway placement, catalog or config refresh) arrives while the publication is reserving its rows. The agent then sees an unpushed head and publishes again.

## User Impact

User impact: publishing from a busy Gateway no longer fails for no reason and no longer leads to a second publish attempt. This mostly affects subagent sessions and sessions that have running subagents. A real change to the session, its sharing, its workspace or the requester still stops the publication.

## Why This Change Was Made

Every publication step prepares a source capability. That capability is revoked if the session changes before the state worker reserves its rows. The revocation listened to every session notification, including display-only ones: subagent run progress for this session, and Gateway-wide `subagent-runs`, `worker-placements`, `worker-environments`, `catalog` and `config` refreshes. None of these change the rows the source captured. One arriving between preparing the source and reserving it refused the publication; on an isolated Gateway that window measured 2–73 ms per publication.

The listener now applies the existing `sessionChangeScopeAffectsStoredRows` filter. Sibling authority owners already use the same filter, for example worktree owner protection, transcript authority and delivery generation. The following still revoke the source:

- stored-row changes and session-store topology changes;
- profile changes, which go through the listener that already exists for them.

The worker still rechecks every captured source fact under its reservation, including the placement row. The grant also rechecks the requester policy.

<details>
<summary>Investigation: the two reported double publishes</summary>

- **Oct 28, 03:30 UTC, subagent session, PR #186455.** The first `github_publish` handoff resumed the session about 4 seconds later with `{"ok":false,"error":"GitHub publication source authority changed.","code":"UNAVAILABLE"}`. The PR head was still the old commit, so nothing had been pushed. The resumed turn retried once, which was the correct response to that result, and the retry published. The deployed build already holds back other turns during the handoff (`fenceSuccessors: true`, since #178756). The only turn between the two attempts was the one that received the failed result, so this was not a concurrent publish. The later `workspacePath is only available for local host publication` error is a separate issue: `edit` never accepts `workspacePath`, and the message is misleading. It has a different owner and is not changed here.
- **Oct 28, 05:16 UTC, PR #186541.** There was no second publish. A human message, queued at 04:05, ran after the publication had already pushed but before its result event. The handoff releases queued successors in FIFO order before it enqueues the result. That turn read the published head with `edit`, and the result arrived afterwards as a late receipt. This ordering is intended and is not changed.
- Team transcripts show the same refusal in at least five other handoff publications on Oct 27 and 28. Of the four failing sessions I checked, three were subagent sessions. Gateway logs do not record which notification revoked the source. The trigger is therefore inferred from the mechanism and the reproduction below, not observed directly.
- Related: #186321 fixed a different false refusal ("session authority changed during snapshot"). #186541 changes handoff completion delivery. Neither overlaps this change.

</details>

## Evidence

- **New coordinator regression** in `github-publication-boundaries.test.ts`: `publishes while subagent progress and placement refreshes keep notifying`. It uses the real publication coordinator and SQLite state with mocked git and GitHub commands, and keeps sending keyed subagent progress and global placement refreshes during the publish. On `main` it fails with the production error, raised by the session-change revoke. It passes with this change.
- **New owner test** in `github-publication.worker.test.ts`. A prepared source now survives the real `publishSubagentRunChanges` producer (keyed and global) and a `worker-placements` refresh, and inserts its row. A stored `session-entry` change still revokes it. The test fails on `main` and passes with this change.
- Both test files pass in full: 35 of 35 and 19 of 19.
- `pnpm check:changed` passes for typecheck (core and core tests) and its ratchets. Its first run found two lint issues and one format issue in the new test, which are now fixed; the oxlint and format checks pass on all three changed files. The dead-export scan still fails on unused exports that already exist in files this PR doesn't touch (`extensions/knowledge/src/page-budget.ts`, `src/cli/completion-runtime.ts` and `src/infra/diagnostic-model-call-types.ts`).
- Independent AutoReview (Codex `gpt-6.1-sol`, P0–P2) on the committed range found nothing actionable. It confirmed that the worker rereads session, membership, placement, profile, connection, workspace and worktree facts under its reservation.
- **Live isolated Gateway on Crabbox (one AWS lease, released): the false refusal did not reproduce on base.** Base is `origin/main` `c14ee716` (includes #186541). After is the same tree with only `src/gateway/github-publication-source.ts` replaced by this PR's file, byte-identical to head `491e8a0`. Every run starts a real Gateway with isolated state and a WebChat operator client. A scripted model calls the real `github_publish` tool with `workspacePath`, so the real handoff, workspace adoption, coordinator, source authority and SQLite worker all run. Real `git` and `gh` then push the branch and open the PR.
  - **Faked:** the model (a scripted Responses server) and GitHub itself: an HTTPS fixture serves the `api.github.com` REST calls and `git http-backend` serves `github.com`, reached through `/etc/hosts` and a lease-local CA. No real repository, token or `roboclaw-bot` credential was used.
  - **Counts** (published out of counted runs; each run's first publication is an uncounted warm-up):

    | Scenario, all traffic from real Gateway activity | Base | After |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | Busy Gateway: 3 concurrent publishers, each with 2 running subagents, plus 2 sessions continuously spawning subagents; the WebChat client watches each publisher's PR rows | 20/20 | 20/20 |
    | A subagent publishes (incident A shape), 3 concurrent | 9/9 | 9/9 |
    | Stored-row writes: label edits on the publishing session every ~15 ms during the publication | 9/10 (the 10th: `Session event owner is being deleted`); warm-up refused with `source authority changed` | 9/10 (the 10th: `Session event owner is being deleted`); warm-up refused with `source authority changed` |
    | Negative: `sessions.reset` while the publication's base-branch read is held | 0/5 PRs created | 0/5 PRs created |

  - **Why base did not fail:** in a diagnostic copy of the base file (not shipped), each publication prepared one durable source, open for 2–73 ms before its reservation. Across 31 instrumented publications, 240 session notifications arrived inside these windows, and none was Gateway-wide or keyed to the publishing session, so none revoked. On an isolated Gateway I could not produce the notification classes this change filters inside that window at a meaningful rate. Worker placement and environment refreshes need cloud worker environments, and `config.patch` is rate-limited to a few writes per minute. The production trigger is still inferred, not observed.
  - **What the live run does show:** the harness observes the exact production refusal through the real tool path. On both trees, label edits keyed to the publishing session revoked the source with `GitHub publication source authority changed.` Real stored-row changes still cancel a publication on both trees.
  - **Separate finding, not changed here:** on both trees, a publication's handoff sometimes failed with `Session event owner is being deleted`. The first `workspacePath` publication on a fresh Gateway failed this way in 6 of the 9 runs without subagent activity; in the other 3, the stored-row edits refused it first. It also failed this way once later in a run, after stored-row edits. When subagents were active, the first publication succeeded. No PR was created. This is a second false refusal that also invites a retry. It needs its own investigation.

<details>
<summary>Commands and log excerpts</summary>

The harness is a task proof artifact and is not committed: `test/e2e/qa-lab/runtime/github-publish-authority.proof.e2e.test.ts` plus `publish-proof/{setup,run,matrix}.sh`. It ran from a separate checkout synced to the lease.

```
bash test/e2e/qa-lab/runtime/publish-proof/setup.sh    # gh, fixture CA, unprivileged :443
bash test/e2e/qa-lab/runtime/publish-proof/matrix.sh   # base/after × 4 scenarios, one Gateway per run
```

```
[proof] SUMMARY base-display scenario=parent concurrency=3 watch=true traffic=display [["{\"status\":\"published\"}",20]]
[proof] SUMMARY head-display scenario=parent concurrency=3 watch=true traffic=display [["{\"status\":\"published\"}",20]]
[proof] iteration 0 outcome GitHub publication source authority changed. prCreated=false 5985ms {"ok":false,"error":"GitHub publication source authority changed.","code":"UNAVAILABLE"}   # head-stored warm-up
[source-diag] revoke … admitted=false at …github-publication-source.ts:304 <- notifyListeners <- session-row-changes install <- publishFacts   # label edit on the publishing session, diagnostic copy of the after file
== source windows (prepare -> first revoke, ms)  n=7 min=25 median=46 max=73   # busy Gateway, base diagnostic copy
```

The results archive (`results.jsonl` plus per-run traces) is kept in the implementation session's workspace with sha256 `7fde015ce98feef6114a1dd482da62b35e626134a5c32359138075e0ab5ba24b`.

</details>

## Work sessions

- [Original discussion with @jalehman](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/2429e543-7982-4d97-98a9-e1cd884488e2)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/c8b0f3f7-a291-454b-8fdf-78531ce079d6)

- @jalehman
- @Patrick-Erichsen

prs.title: fix(ci): bound dependency cache cleanup per invocation
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

PR tooling can synchronously remove every excess dependency installation before command dispatch. The retention-policy change in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/184650 preserved the newest four unused installs but dropped the existing per-invocation cleanup limit.

## User Impact

Each materialization removes at most four eligible entries, sharing that budget across unused installations and stale stages. Later invocations drain the backlog. This bounds removal count, not elapsed time; scanning, sorting and an individual deletion can still take time. Production application behavior is unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Restore the cleanup owner's existing incremental behavior without weakening current-entry, live-consumer/creator, ownership, permission, symlink or 24-hour stage protections. Keep the newest-four reuse policy. The materialized-anchor sibling already uses a four-removal limit.

## Evidence

- Independent source/test review, local autoreview and independent documentation review: no actionable findings.
- Shell syntax, embedded JavaScript syntax, targeted test/docs formatting and diff checks passed.
- Explicit Node 26 focused proof: all 5 cases across dependency-cache and materialized-anchor files passed in 4.89s (cache file 3.391s; anchor file 0.079s). The complete original cleanup owner fails both backlog assertions; restoring the exact committed owner passes both.
- Targeted tooling typecheck and lint passed. All 201 exact-head checks are complete with no failures: 59 success, 141 skipped, 1 neutral.
- The documentation change follows the existing downstream R2 publication workflow. Landing remains held for owner confirmation of that publication; do not enable auto-merge.
- Regression tests target disposable fixture caches; no real-cache cleanup experiment or profiling was performed. No measured CI-minute, elapsed-time or invoice saving is claimed.

Production: +5/-0, justified by the foreground cleanup owner's bounded removal invariant. Tests: +31/-9. Docs: +6/-3. No new helper, dependency, cache, timer, retry or compatibility path.

prs.title: fix(update): repair loops on its own error when a crashed update also left a pending package step
prs.body:
Closes #184893

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw update repair` fails with "Another update executor owns this installation ... run `openclaw update repair` to settle it", and every later update stays blocked, when a cancelled updater exited while a package update step it had prepared was still pending.

## User Impact

Repair now settles both leftovers in one run: the unused package preparation closes as `publication-not-started` (the installed package and launchers stay unchanged), the cancelled update custody is released, and the next `openclaw update` is admitted. Before, repair told the user to run repair, and every repair refused the same way.

## Why This Change Was Made

Repair settled the pending package step first, and that settlement asked for fresh update admission. The cancelled custody refuses fresh admission by design, and repair only replaces that custody with its own claim in a later step, so it never got there.

Repair now takes its claim first and settles the package step under it. Finalization already runs repair's maintenance under the same claim, so this adds no new authority. Settlement keeps its own executor admission when no claim is held (ordinary repair with no leftover custody, and the update command's own settlement).

Scope of the claim: repair holds it for both kinds of leftover lock it settles, the cancelled custody of a crashed updater (lease version 4) and an older dead owner it reclaims (version 2 triage or legacy update child). A dead triage owner refuses fresh admission the same way (existing test "repair reclaims a root handoff owner"), so a pending package step settles under the claim there too. Legacy update children go through the same path but are not separately tested, and no test combines either older kind with a pending package step.

Known edge: an earlier macOS Gateway keeps its own lease store. When the custody sits there, repair's claim lives in that store rather than the one the package step recorded; settlement still checks the recorded lease database identity, and admission in the current store stays fenced by the earlier store's check (#185002). Low risk, not separately tested.

Unchanged: when the custody cannot be settled yet (its updater or descendants still live, or the grace period has not passed), repair still refuses as before; the next repair settles both once the custody is free.

## Evidence

**Regression through the registered `openclaw update repair` CLI**, `update-repair-cancellation.test.ts` "repair settles cancelled custody together with an unused package preparation". A real updater process prepares the package step, cancels, and dies by SIGKILL (the existing crash fixture), leaving a version 4 lease family of 4 rows and a `prepared` journal. The only synthetic piece is the inert sealed helper the journal records, as in the existing package activation tests.

- On `main` (b0966db1204): repair exits 1 with "Another update executor owns this installation. It retains cancelled update custody (owner …, lease version 4, …). If that update has exited, run openclaw update repair to settle it."; all 4 custody rows remain; the next admission is refused the same way.
- With this change: repair exits 0 (`status: "ok"`), reports "previous package update operation … closed as publication-not-started. The original package and launchers remain unchanged.", leaves 0 custody rows and no pending package step, and the next admission succeeds.
- The 6 existing cases in that file pass on both, including the failed and deferred repair cases that keep the claim.

**A lost claim changes nothing.** `package-update-activation-retirement.test.ts` "preserves damaged unused helper|candidate while settling an unpublished preparation" now first settles under a repair claim whose check throws: settlement rejects with that error before any report (the case's later call count proves none ran), and the journal stays `prepared`; the ordinary settlement then proceeds as before. On `main` the claim is ignored and settlement proceeds, so both rows fail.

**Bench run (isolated container with an init process, main `b0966db1204` vs this head):** the two changed test files give main 3 failures, exactly the new checks (both lost-claim rows and the combined repair case), and this change 15/15. Without an init process the container's first shell does not reap the SIGKILLed test updater, so repair sees "Handoff descendants remain live or unverified" and the existing crash cases fail on both refs alike; that is a property of the container, not of this change.

**Checks.** The 48 test files that import the repair command or package activation pass (702 tests); `pnpm tsgo:core` and `pnpm tsgo:core:test` pass; oxlint and oxfmt are clean on the changed files. Net test lines against the merge base: 0. The repeated retained-custody and settled-custody report checks in `update-repair-cancellation.test.ts` moved into two helpers, the earlier-Gateway store setup into a third, and the inert sealed-helper mock is now exported from the activation lifetime fixture; every assertion is kept. Re-proof after the consolidation on the bench (one tree at a time, init process): `main` fails exactly the 3 new checks (both lost-claim rows and the combined repair case, for the bug's reasons), this branch 15/15; on the Mac the 15 test files that use the changed fixture pass except 5 pre-existing child-process cases in `package-update-activation-lifetime.test.ts` that need a built sealed helper and fail the same way on the previous head.

**Live proof with a real installed package** (isolated bench, Debian container with an init process, Node 26). Both refs were packed with `scripts/package-openclaw-for-docker.mjs` (`main` at 6bd45e1ba98, and this branch at 2eec3e631d5 merged onto it; the later commit 1fb2a67ded6 changes test files only), installed with npm, and updated with `openclaw update --tag <newer local package> --timeout 1800`. The update ran under libfaketime with a timestamp file. The moment its package activation journal reached `prepared`, the clock was advanced by 1800 s, so the update's own deadline expired inside the step between preparation and publication (where a real install stops and drains the Gateway; in the container that step takes well under a second, which is why the clock had to move). The real deadline cancelled the update: "Package activation was refused and its prepared publication could not be retired. | Update activation exceeded its 1799-second budget." It recorded cancelled custody (lease version 4) while the journal stayed `prepared`, and a watcher sent SIGKILL the instant that row appeared, like a crash during cancellation cleanup. State after the crash on every lane: 1 custody row (version 4), journal `prepared`, no leftover or zombie processes. Later commands ran on the same advanced clock: +31 min for the next update, +80 min for repair and the final update, past the 45-minute custody grace. Repair's process census refuses inside a detected container by design ("Host process visibility cannot be established from this container"), so each lane removed the Docker marker before starting; the install's processes all live in that container's own PID namespace, which shares nothing.

- On `main` (3 lanes, all alike): next update exit 1, "Another update executor owns this installation. It retains cancelled update custody (owner …, lease version 4, …). If that update has exited, run openclaw update repair to settle it."; repair exit 1 with that same message, twice; the custody row and the pending package step remain; the final update exit 1 with the same message. That is the reported loop.
- With this change (1 lane): next update exit 1 with the same refusal (unchanged); repair exit 0 and "previous package update operation … closed as publication-not-started. The original package and launchers remain unchanged."; afterwards 0 custody rows and no pending package step; a second repair exit 0; the final update exit 0 and installed the newer package.
- Boundary, with this change and without the kill (1 lane): the same cancelled update, left to exit on its own, released its custody itself ("Cancellation settled before recovery"; 0 rows, journal `prepared`), and the next update recovered the package step and finished (exit 0). The loop needs the updater to die after recording its cancellation, which is the crashed updater the issue describes.
- Not counted: in rounds of six lanes at once, some updates stalled at the candidate Gateway start-up check before reaching the package step and never produced the state; the three-lane `main` round had no stalls.

Earlier live attempts, for the record: a plain kill (TERM, then KILL) at `prepared` never records cancelled custody; the next update reclaims the dead owner and recovers the package step on both refs. Only the deadline writes cancelled custody. Git-checkout installs do not create a package step, so they cannot reach this path.

### Live run

Captured lane summaries (timestamps are the bench's real clock; `<prefix>` is the npm prefix of the install). `main`:

```
[20:49:04] installed version 2026.10.8 -> target 2026.10.9
2026-10-28T20:52:49.642Z phase prepared
2026-10-28T20:52:49.642Z clock jumped +1800
[20:52:49] cancelled custody recorded 180s after start; update killed: {"key":"<prefix>/lib/node_modules/openclaw","rows":1}
[20:52:51] update exit 137
[20:52:51] lease rows after crash: [{"root":"<prefix>/lib/node_modules/openclaw","version":4}]
[20:52:51] journal phase after crash: [{"phase":"prepared"}]
[20:52:53] next update exit 1
Another update executor owns this installation. It retains cancelled update custody (owner c78f50d7-12f7-4664-924c-24f40c42b100, lease version 4, last activity 2026-10-28T21:22:49.661Z). If that update has exited, run openclaw update repair to settle it.
[20:52:56] repair 1 exit 1
Another update executor owns this installation. It retains cancelled update custody (owner c78f50d7-12f7-4664-924c-24f40c42b100, lease version 4, last activity 2026-10-28T21:22:49.661Z). If that update has exited, run openclaw update repair to settle it.
[20:52:58] repair 2 exit 1
Another update executor owns this installation. It retains cancelled update custody (owner c78f50d7-12f7-4664-924c-24f40c42b100, lease version 4, last activity 2026-10-28T21:22:49.661Z). If that update has exited, run openclaw update repair to settle it.
[20:52:58] lease rows after repair: [{"root":"<prefix>/lib/node_modules/openclaw","version":4}]
[20:52:58] pending journal after repair: 1
[20:53:00] final update exit 1
Another update executor owns this installation. It retains cancelled update custody (owner c78f50d7-12f7-4664-924c-24f40c42b100, lease version 4, last activity 2026-10-28T21:22:49.661Z). If that update has exited, run openclaw update repair to settle it.
[20:53:00] installed version now: OpenClaw 2026.10.8
```

With this change:

```
[20:24:50] installed version 2026.10.8 -> target 2026.10.9
2026-10-28T20:31:20.878Z phase prepared
2026-10-28T20:31:20.878Z clock jumped +1800
[20:31:20] cancelled custody recorded 318s after start; update killed: {"key":"<prefix>/lib/node_modules/openclaw","rows":1}
[20:31:23] update exit 137
Package activation was refused and its prepared publication could not be retired. | Update activation exceeded its 1799.779133255-second budget.
[20:31:23] lease rows after crash: [{"root":"<prefix>/lib/node_modules/openclaw","version":4}]
[20:31:23] journal phase after crash: [{"phase":"prepared"}]
[20:31:25] next update exit 1
Another update executor owns this installation. It retains cancelled update custody (owner 2c3812d9-6faa-4ea5-a6ad-aee53724c049, lease version 4, last activity 2026-10-28T21:01:20.905Z). If that update has exited, run openclaw update repair to settle it.
[20:36:51] repair 1 exit 0
"status": "ok"
closed as publication-not-started
[20:38:09] repair 2 exit 0
[20:38:09] lease rows after repair: []
[20:38:09] pending journal after repair: 0
[20:45:13] final update exit 0
[20:45:13] installed version now: OpenClaw 2026.10.9
```

### Upgrade from the latest stable release with existing settings and data

Stored data: this change touches no schema, journal, lease row, report or config format. It changes the order of two steps in repair and adds an in-process `owner` option to settlement; everything written to disk is written by the same code as before.

Run (same bench, 2 lanes alike): the published `openclaw@2026.10.8` (npm `latest`, build dc2523e) was installed from the registry, given a config with user settings (`plugins.enabled=false`, `update.channel=stable`, `agents.defaults.model`, `gateway.port`) and a workspace file, then updated to this branch's package (2026.10.9) with `openclaw update --tag <local package>`; `openclaw update repair` ran twice on the upgraded install; a final `openclaw update` ran; then the data was checked.

```
[21:02:29] openclaw --version: OpenClaw 2026.10.8 (dc2523e) (installed from openclaw@2026.10.8)
[21:02:32] config validate before update exit 0
[21:09:40] next update exit 0
[21:10:42] repair 1 exit 0
[21:11:42] repair 2 exit 0
[21:11:42] pending journal after repair: 0
[21:13:04] final update exit 0
[21:13:04] installed version now: OpenClaw 2026.10.9
[21:13:06] config validate after exit 0
[21:13:07] workspace seed readable: seeded before update 2026-10-28T21:02:29
[21:13:07] state files after: 16; missing from before: 0
[21:13:12] update status after exit 0
```

After the upgrade every user setting is still in the config, byte for byte; the update's own doctor added its usual bookkeeping (`agents.entries.main`, `meta.migrations`, `meta.lastTouchedVersion`, `wizard`), which is the same on `main`. `openclaw doctor --json` (read-only lint) on the upgraded install: 41 checks run, 4 warnings, all about the minimal config (gateway token and mode unset, legacy browser relay auth, a retained pre-migration snapshot), no errors. `openclaw update status --json` reads the recorded runs. The crash-and-repair path was not exercised from the released build: when the published 2026.10.8 drives the update, the clock jump did not cancel it (the journal went straight to `publication-complete`), so the loop itself was shown only with both refs packed from source, above.

prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Windows repair package-owner test fixture shells out to system tar for every synthetic archive. Its existing "without system tar" test restricts PATH only after archive creation, hiding that dependency.

## User Impact

The fixture creates fresh gzip archives through the existing tar dependency and waits for archive closure before removing the lifecycle marker. The no-system-tools check now covers fixture creation too. Production behavior is unchanged.

## Evidence

- Source review: 23 fixture archive calls per complete 24-case file; external fixture tar launches become zero. This is a source-derived process count, not a timing or billing measurement.
- Fresh files and archives remain independent per case. Real Node loader/import-hook processes, package-member authentication, tamper, symlink, missing-member, oversized and compressible-member coverage stay intact.
- The separate real npm pack and offline install case is unchanged.
- Independent source review and local autoreview: no actionable findings. Awaited tar.create completion matches the installed dependency contract.
- Current head passes all 24 cases on explicitly selected Node. Baseline-red/candidate-green no-tools controls pass on Node and pinned Bun. Earlier tooling checks passed; the one-line PATH follow-up has fresh independent source review and formatting proof. Local empty-PATH behavior was traced to Bun host-tool fallback, so the case uses a fresh empty directory. Performance qualification below holds promotion.

Production LOC delta: 0. Tests: +5/-8 (net -3). No new helper, dependency, cache, fixture reuse, timeout or retry.

## Prospective Performance Rule

Record this rule before any timed run. Compare the complete committed baseline and candidate 24-case file on the same Mac host, Node version, frozen dependencies and environment, using the repository test wrapper with one worker and OPENCLAW_VITEST_RUNTIME=node explicitly selected on both sides. Keep each side's existing real npm pack/offline-install case and all independent archive creation inside the timed workload.

Run one untimed warm-up per side, then five serial alternating A/B pairs. Report every pair plus wall time, user CPU, system CPU and peak RSS median, empirical nearest-rank p95, and min/max spread; verify both sides pass the same 24 cases. Do not run other task-owned checks concurrently with timing.

Every measured surface must hold or improve. A regression of 20% or more stops promotion; smaller adverse results hold this draft for explanation rather than being rounded away.
